# Dot Com Immigration, full context

## What this practice is

A Canadian immigration practice whose work centres on matters with statutory deadlines, run by
Angad Sachdeva, who holds an RCIC-IRB licence from the College of Immigration and Citizenship
Consultants. The RCIC-IRB class is the one permitted to appear before the Immigration and Refugee
Board of Canada. Services are offered in English and French.

## Scope of the licence, stated precisely

CAN do, before the Immigration and Refugee Board:
- Refugee claims at the Refugee Protection Division
- Refugee appeals at the Refugee Appeal Division
- Detention reviews and admissibility hearings at the Immigration Division
- Sponsorship, removal order and residency obligation appeals at the Immigration Appeal Division

CAN do, in applications to IRCC and CBSA:
- Family sponsorship, permanent residence, work and study permits, visitor visas,
  temporary resident permits, criminal rehabilitation, authorisation to return to Canada,
  humanitarian and compassionate applications, citizenship applications,
  pre-removal risk assessments, responses to procedural fairness letters

CANNOT do:
- Represent anyone in a judicial review at the Federal Court. Only a lawyer may do that.
  Neither consultants nor paralegals can. This is stated openly on the site.

## Verified deadline information published on the site

Refugee Appeal Division, Notice of Appeal: generally 15 days from receiving the written reasons.
The clock runs from receipt of the reasons, not the hearing date and not the date printed on the
decision. Source: Immigration and Refugee Board, Filing a refugee appeal.

Refugee Appeal Division, perfecting the appeal: the RAD Rules set 30 days. A practice notice issued
in September 2020 extended the period and was stated to remain in force until further notice. The
site does not quote a fixed figure for this and directs users to confirm against the current notice.

Detention reviews, Immigration Division: the reasons for detention are reviewed within 48 hours of
detention or as soon as possible afterwards; if continued detention is ordered, a further review
within seven days; thereafter at least once every 30 days. An earlier review may be requested on new
facts. Source: Immigration and Refugee Board, Detention review process.

Bill C-12 (Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act): royal assent 26 March 2026.
Introduces a one year bar on referral to the Refugee Protection Division for claims made more than
one year after first entry, applied retroactively to 24 June 2020, and a 14 day bar for irregular
entrants from the United States. Around 30,000 people were notified they may be ineligible.
Those barred may still be able to seek a pre-removal risk assessment.

Proposed asylum regulations, June 2026: would give claimants 60 days to submit a complete
application with one 30 day extension. These are PROPOSED and the site labels them as such.

## Published statistics cited on the site

- 259,085 refugee claims pending at the Board, August 2026 (IRB volume reports)
- About 24 months from referral to decision as of December 2025 (IRB, CIMM March 2026)
- Refugee Appeal Division wait about 4 months; Immigration Appeal Division about 6 months
- 2025: 12,339 refugee appeals filed; 10,955 finalised; of 9,910 decided on the merits,
  6,865 dismissed and 3,045 allowed, about 31 per cent
- 2025: 107,802 refugee claims referred; 79,462 finalised; 14,619 rejected
- Sponsorship appeals filed: 2,495 in 2024, 3,360 in 2025
- Immigration appeals finalised 2025: 3,935, of which 1,426 allowed
- CBSA removals: 23,160 in 2025; 14,897 in January to August 2026
- CBSA detention 2025: 3,598 people detained, average 18 days, median 5 days;
  1,380 released on an alternative to detention

## Regulatory context the site relies on

The CICC regulatory framework was overhauled on 15 July 2026. The public register now shows whether
a licensee is in good standing and any disciplinary history, penalties were increased, and a
compensation fund was created for clients who lose money through a licensee's theft, fraud,
misappropriation or misrepresentation. Eligibility requires a formal CICC complaint, a discipline
committee finding, a dishonest act committed on or after 23 November 2021, that the client was not
complicit, and a final decision issued on or after 15 July 2026. The site describes this accurately
and does not present it as a general refund scheme.

Legal Aid Ontario certificates can only be billed by roster lawyers. Immigration consultants cannot
bill them. The practice therefore prices discrete pieces of work rather than only full retainers.

## Advertising compliance

Under the Code of Professional Conduct for CICC Licensees, SOR/2022-128, sections 44 to 46, a
website is a written advertisement. It must display the licensee's registered name and the College
public register's internet address, must not make false or misleading representations, must not
guarantee success, and must not suggest a connection with government. Client testimonials require
written authorisation under section 45.

## Service tiers

1. Free deadline triage: send the document, receive the date.
2. Options assessment, fixed fee.
3. Decision or document review, fixed fee.
4. Discrete tasks, priced per task: Notice of Appeal filed, record prepared, submissions written.
5. Full representation on retainer.
